paragraphs: This was the visit that Grushenka had described to Rakitin with such horror. She was waiting just then for the “message,” and she was hugely relieved that Mitya had not turned up either that day or the day before. She had been hoping that “please God he won’t come till I’m gone,” and now here he was, bursting in on her. The rest we know already. To get rid of him, she proposed right away that he walk with her to Samsonov’s, where she said she simply had to go “to settle his accounts.” Mitya went along at once, and at the gate she said good-by, making him promise to come at twelve o’clock and take her home. Mitya was delighted with this arrangement too. If she was sitting at Samsonov’s, she could not be off to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s, “if only she’s not lying,” he added immediately. Still, judging by what he had seen, he thought she was not lying.

He was the kind of jealous man who, while the woman he loves is out of sight, dreams up every sort of dreadful picture of what may be happening to her and how she may be betraying him. Then, shaken and heartbroken and certain of her faithlessness, he runs back to her. But one look at her face, that gay, laughing, affectionate face, and he comes back to life. He drops every suspicion and, with joyful shame, calls himself names for having been jealous.
Once he had left Grushenka at the gate, he hurried home. Oh, there was so much still to do that day! But at least a weight had been lifted from his heart.

“Now I only have to rush and find out from Smerdyakov whether anything happened over there last night, whether she, by any chance, went to Fyodor Pavlovitch; ugh!” the thought flashed through his mind.
He had not even reached his lodging before jealousy was boiling up again in his restless heart.

Jealousy! “Othello was not jealous, he was trustful,” said Pushkin. That one remark is enough to show how deeply our great poet saw. Othello’s soul was shattered and his whole view of the world went dark simply because _his ideal was destroyed_. But Othello did not go hiding, spying, peeping. Quite the opposite: he was trustful. It took enormous effort to lead him along, push him, and work him up before he would even consider the idea of deceit. The truly jealous man is not like that. No one can imagine the shame and moral degradation a jealous man will sink to without a twinge of conscience. And it is not as if all the jealous were vulgar, base souls. A man of lofty feelings, whose love is pure and full of self-sacrifice, may nevertheless hide under tables, bribe the vilest people, and become well acquainted with the lowest disgrace of spying and eavesdropping.

Othello could not bring himself to accept faithlessness. He was not unable to forgive it; he was unable to accept it, though his soul was as innocent and free of malice as a baby’s. The truly jealous man is different. It is hard to imagine what some jealous men can bring themselves to accept and overlook, and what they can forgive! The jealous are the quickest of all to forgive, and every woman knows it. A jealous man can forgive astonishingly fast (after a violent scene, naturally). He can forgive unfaithfulness that is all but proved, even the very kisses and embraces he has seen with his own eyes, so long as he can somehow be persuaded that it was all “for the last time,” and that his rival will disappear from that day on and go off to the ends of the earth, or that he himself will take her away to some place the dreaded rival can never get near. Of course the peace lasts only an hour. For even if the rival did vanish the next day, he would invent another and be jealous of him. And you might ask what kind of love it is that has to be watched so closely, and what a love is worth if it needs such hard guarding. But the jealous will never understand that. And yet there are men of noble heart among them. It is remarkable, too, that these very men of noble heart, standing hidden in some cupboard, listening and spying, never feel a sting of conscience at that moment, at any rate, though with their “noble hearts” they understand perfectly well what shameful depths they have chosen to sink to.

When Mitya saw Grushenka, his jealousy vanished. For a moment he became trustful and generous and actually despised himself for his evil thoughts. But that only proved that his love for her held something far higher than he himself suspected, that it was not merely sensual passion, not merely the “curve of her body” he had talked to Alyosha about. Yet the moment Grushenka was gone, Mitya started suspecting her of every low trick of faithlessness, and he felt no sting of conscience over that either.

So jealousy was boiling up in him again. In any case he had to hurry. The first thing was to get hold of some money, even a small loan, just for the time being. The nine roubles had nearly all been spent on his trip. And, as we all know, you can’t take a step without money. But on the cart he had worked out where he could get a loan. He owned a fine pair of dueling pistols in a case, which he had never pawned until now, because he valued them more than anything else he had.

Some time ago, at the “Metropolis” tavern, he had got to know a young official, and had learned that this extremely well-off bachelor was passionately fond of weapons. The man bought pistols, revolvers and daggers, hung them on his wall, and showed them off to his acquaintances. He was proud of the collection and was something of a specialist in how a revolver works. Mitya went straight to him without a second thought and offered to pawn his pistols for ten roubles. The official was delighted and began urging him to sell them outright. Mitya would not hear of it, so the young man handed over ten roubles, insisting that nothing would make him charge interest. They parted as friends.

Mitya was in a rush. He hurried toward Fyodor Pavlovitch’s by the back way, to the arbor, hoping to catch Smerdyakov as soon as he could. So it is on record that three or four hours before a certain event, which I will describe later, Mitya did not have a farthing and pawned a treasured possession for ten roubles, although three hours after that he held thousands in his hands.... But I am running ahead of my story. From Marya Kondratyevna (the woman who lived next to Fyodor Pavlovitch) he got the very disturbing news that Smerdyakov was ill. She told him the story of the fall in the cellar, the fit, the doctor’s visit, and Fyodor Pavlovitch’s worry. He also heard, with interest, that his brother Ivan had left that morning for Moscow.

“So he must have driven through Volovya ahead of me,” thought Dmitri, but he was terribly upset about Smerdyakov. “What now? Who’ll keep watch for me? Who’ll bring me word?” he thought. He started eagerly asking the women whether they had seen anything the evening before. They knew exactly what he was after, and they put his mind completely at rest. Nobody had been there. Ivan Fyodorovitch had been there that night, and everything had gone just as usual. Mitya fell to thinking. He would certainly have to stand watch today, but where? Here, or at Samsonov’s gate? He decided he had to keep a lookout in both places, and meanwhile ... meanwhile.... The trouble was that he had a new plan, worked out on the way back, that he had to carry out. He was sure it would work, but he could not put it off. Mitya decided to spend an hour on it: “In an hour I’ll know everything, I’ll have everything settled, and then, then, first of all to Samsonov’s. I’ll ask whether Grushenka’s there and come straight back here, wait till eleven, and then go to Samsonov’s again to bring her home.” That was what he decided.

He flew home, washed, combed his hair, brushed his clothes, changed, and set off for Madame Hohlakov’s. Alas! It was on her that he had pinned his hopes. He had made up his mind to borrow three thousand from that lady. And, what is more, he suddenly felt sure that she would not turn him down. One may well ask why, if he was so certain, he had not gone to her first, to someone of his own kind, so to speak, rather than to Samsonov, a man he did not know, who belonged to another class, and who was someone he hardly knew how to talk to.

The truth was that he had never really known Madame Hohlakov, that he had not seen her for a month, and that he knew she could not bear him. She had disliked him from the very beginning because he was engaged to Katerina Ivanovna, whereas she had suddenly, for no clear reason, set her heart on Katerina Ivanovna jilting him and marrying the “charming, chivalrously refined Ivan, who had such excellent manners.” Mitya’s manners she loathed. Mitya openly laughed at her, and had once remarked that she was as lively and at ease in company as she was uneducated. But that morning in the cart a brilliant idea had come to him: “If she’s so keen that I shouldn’t marry Katerina Ivanovna” (and he knew she was positively hysterical on the subject) “why would she refuse me that three thousand now, so that I can drop Katya and get away from her for good? These spoiled society ladies, once they’ve set their hearts on something, will spare no expense to indulge a whim. Besides, she’s so rich,” Mitya reasoned.

His “plan” was exactly the same as before: he would offer his rights to Tchermashnya. But this time it was not as a business proposition, as it had been with Samsonov, not luring the lady with a possible profit of six or seven thousand, but only as security for the loan. As he worked out this new idea, Mitya was thrilled with it, but that was how he always felt about all his undertakings and all his sudden decisions. He threw himself into every new idea with passionate enthusiasm. Yet as he climbed the steps of Madame Hohlakov’s house, a shiver of fear ran down his spine. In that moment he saw clearly, with the certainty of a mathematical proof, that this was his last hope, and that if it failed, there was nothing left for him in the world except to “rob and murder someone for the three thousand.” It was half-past seven when he rang the bell.

At first luck seemed to be on his side. The moment his name was announced, he was received with remarkable speed. “As if she’d been waiting for me,” thought Mitya, and no sooner had he been shown into the drawing-room than the lady of the house herself came running in and announced that she had been expecting him.

“I was expecting you! I was expecting you! I had no reason at all to think you would come to see me, as you must admit yourself. But I did expect you. You may well marvel at my instinct, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, but all morning I was certain you would come.”

“That is certainly remarkable, madam,” said Mitya, sinking limply into a chair, “but I’ve come to you about something very important.... Something of the utmost importance for me, I mean, madam ... for me alone ... and I’m in a hurry to—”

“I know it’s most important business that brings you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. It isn’t a presentiment, it isn’t any reactionary throwback to the miraculous (have you heard about Father Zossima?). It’s a matter of mathematics: after everything that has passed with Katerina Ivanovna, you couldn’t help coming. You couldn’t, you couldn’t, it’s a mathematical certainty.”
“The realism of real life, madam, that’s what it is. But please let me explain—”
“Realism indeed, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. I’m all for realism now. I’ve had my fill of miracles. Have you heard that Father Zossima is dead?”
“No, madam, this is the first I’ve heard of it.” Mitya was a little startled. Alyosha’s face came into his mind.
“Last night, and just imagine—”

“Madam,” said Mitya, “all I can imagine is that I’m in a desperate position, and that if you don’t help me, everything will fall apart, and I first of all. Forgive the commonplace expression, but I’m in a fever—”

“I know, I know you’re in a fever. How could you not be? And whatever you tell me, I know it in advance. I’ve been thinking about your destiny for a long time, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. I’m watching over it and studying it.... Oh, believe me, I’m an experienced doctor of the soul, Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

“Madam, if you’re an experienced doctor, then I’m certainly an experienced patient,” said Mitya, forcing himself to be polite, “and I feel that if you are watching over my fate like this, you will come to my aid in my ruin. So at least let me lay out for you the plan I’ve dared to bring to you ... and what I’m hoping you will do.... I’ve come, madam—”

“Don’t explain it. It’s of secondary importance. As for help, you’re not the first person I’ve helped, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You’ve most likely heard about my cousin, Madame Belmesov. Her husband was ruined, ‘had come to grief,’ as you so characteristically put it, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. I advised him to go into horse-breeding, and now he’s doing well. Do you know anything about horse-breeding, Dmitri Fyodorovitch?”
